B2-1-0.title: ¿-ing o to + verbo?
B2-1-0.question: ¿Qué palabra va antes del segundo verbo?

branches.if: enjoy, avoid, mind, keep, finish, can’t stand, feel like, consider
branches.example: I feel like going out tonight.

branches.if: Una preposición (on, at, of, for, to en look forward to)
branches.example: I’m looking forward to seeing you.

branches.if: decide, hope, offer, refuse, want, plan
branches.example: She refused to apologise.

branches.use: -ing = acción anterior · to = propósito o deber
branches.example: I stopped to call him. / I stopped calling him.

items.a: I stopped calling him.
items.b: I stopped to call him.
items.note: La primera: dejé de llamarlo. La segunda: me detuve para llamarlo.

items.a: I remember locking the door.
items.b: Remember to lock the door.
items.note: La primera es un recuerdo; la segunda, algo que no debes olvidar hacer.

items.a: I’m looking forward to meeting you.
items.b: I’m looking forward to meet you.
items.note: “To” aquí es preposición: lleva -ing.

B2-1-1.title: De frase simple a cláusula nominal

steps.label: Frase simple
steps.sentence: Nobody apologised.

steps.label: The problem is that…
steps.sentence: **The problem is that** nobody apologised.
steps.change: La cláusula con “that” explica el sujeto.

steps.label: What + be
steps.sentence: **What hurt me was that** nobody apologised.
steps.change: Con “what” al inicio el verbo es singular.

steps.label: The reason… is that…
steps.sentence: **The reason** I’m upset **is that** nobody apologised.

branches.use: The problem / truth / fact is that…
branches.example: The truth is that I miss them.

branches.if: Algo que no se sabe aún
branches.use: The question is what / how / where…
branches.example: The question is where he went.
The question is whether to call her.
What matters is that we stay close.

items.a: The question is where he went.
items.b: The question is where did he go.
items.note: Dentro de la cláusula, orden de afirmación: sin inversión.

items.a: What worries me is the silence.
items.b: What worries me are the silence.
items.note: Con una cláusula con “what” como sujeto, el verbo va en singular.

items.a: The reason is that I was tired.
items.b: The reason is because I was tired.
items.note: Se prefiere “the reason is that”; “because” resulta redundante.

items.example: You should have told me. (You didn’t.)
She was supposed to lock it. (She didn’t.)
We didn’t have to pay. (Probably we didn’t.)
I needn’t have cooked. (I did, but it wasn’t necessary.)
You shouldn’t have shouted. (You did.)
We had to leave early. (We did.)

branches.example: We had to show our passports.
We didn’t have to wear a suit.

branches.if: Lo hiciste, pero no era necesario
branches.example: I needn’t have brought a gift.

branches.if: No se hizo y lo lamentas o lo criticas
branches.example: I should have told the manager.
He was supposed to lock the door.

items.a: You didn’t have to pay.
items.b: You shouldn’t have paid.
items.note: La primera: no era necesario. La segunda: fue un error pagar.

items.a: I didn’t have to bring food.
items.b: I needn’t have brought food.
items.note: La primera sugiere que no llevaste; la segunda dice que llevaste sin necesidad.

items.a: We had to leave.
items.b: We must leave.
items.note: “Must” no tiene pasado: para obligación pasada usa “had to”.

items.example: It can’t have been the cat.
He couldn’t have known.
She might not have seen it.
They could have missed the bus.
They might have taken the wrong turn.
They’ll have landed by now.
He must have forgotten his keys.

steps.label: Pista
steps.sentence: His coat is still on the chair.

steps.label: Casi seguro
steps.sentence: He **must have left** in a hurry.

steps.label: Posible
steps.sentence: He **might have gone** out for lunch.

steps.label: Descartado
steps.sentence: He **can’t have gone** home — it’s raining.

items.a: He could have missed the bus.
items.b: I could have helped, but nobody asked.
items.note: La primera es una posibilidad sobre el pasado; la segunda, una capacidad que no se usó.

items.a: She can’t have known.
items.b: She mustn’t have known.
items.note: El negativo de “must have” (deducción) es “can’t have”.

items.a: He must have forgotten.
items.b: He must of forgotten.
items.note: “Must of” es un error de escritura: se pronuncia /əv/ pero se escribe “have”.

items.a: The guide who showed us around was brilliant.
items.b: Carlos, who showed us around, was brilliant.
items.note: Sin comas identifica cuál guía; con comas, solo agrega información sobre alguien ya identificado.

items.a: My sister who lives in Lima is a nurse.
items.b: My sister, who lives in Lima, is a nurse.
items.note: Sin comas: tengo varias hermanas. Con comas: tengo una sola.

items.a: The city (that) we visited was cold.
items.b: Bogotá, which we visited, was cold.
items.note: Solo en la definitoria puedes omitir el pronombre o usar “that”.

branches.example: The woman who called is my aunt.
Bogotá, which is in the Andes, is cold.
The street where I grew up has changed.
That was the year when everything changed.
The man whose car was stolen called the police.

steps.label: Dos frases
steps.sentence: The district was lovely. We stayed in it.

steps.label: Informal
steps.sentence: The district **(that) we stayed in** was lovely.

steps.label: Formal
steps.sentence: The district **in which we stayed** was lovely.

steps.label: Con where
steps.sentence: The district **where we stayed** was lovely.

steps.label: Sustantivo
steps.sentence: a **bridge**

steps.label: + material
steps.sentence: a **stone** bridge
steps.change: El material va justo antes del sustantivo.

steps.label: + edad
steps.sentence: an **old** stone bridge
steps.change: La edad va antes del material.

steps.label: + opinión y tamaño
steps.sentence: a **lovely little** old stone bridge

items.a: a big old house
items.b: an old big house
items.note: El tamaño va antes de la edad.

items.a: a beautiful red Colombian bag
items.b: a red beautiful Colombian bag
items.note: La opinión va antes del color.

items.a: a red and white facade
items.b: a red white facade
items.note: Dos adjetivos del mismo tipo (colores) se unen con “and”.

branches.example: Despite the traffic, we loved it.
Despite the fact that it rained, we went out.
Although it rained, we explored.

branches.if: Una oración nueva, después de punto o punto y coma
branches.use: however / nevertheless / on the other hand
branches.example: It’s expensive; however, it’s worth it.

steps.label: Despite
steps.sentence: **Despite the noise**, the neighbourhood is lively.

steps.label: Although
steps.sentence: **Although it’s noisy**, the neighbourhood is lively.

steps.label: However
steps.sentence: The neighbourhood is noisy. **However**, it’s lively.

items.example: It was expensive, though.
It’s small. However, it’s cosy.
Although it’s small, it’s cosy.
Despite its size, it’s cosy.
Even though it’s tiny, we love it.
It was risky. Nevertheless, we did it.

steps.label: Cláusula completa
steps.sentence: **While I was waiting** for the bus, I answered my emails.
steps.change: Mismo sujeto en las dos partes: I.

steps.label: Reducida
steps.sentence: **While waiting** for the bus, I answered my emails.
steps.change: Quita el sujeto y el auxiliar; usa -ing.

steps.label: Con before
steps.sentence: **Before I go** to bed, I read. → **Before going** to bed, I read.

steps.label: Pasiva
steps.sentence: **When he was asked**, he agreed. → **When asked**, he agreed.
steps.change: Con pasiva queda solo el participio.

B2-4-0.title: ¿Puedo reducir la cláusula?
B2-4-0.question: ¿Las dos partes tienen el mismo sujeto?

branches.example: After finishing work, she goes to the gym.

branches.if: Sí, y el verbo está en pasiva
branches.example: When asked, she said no.
While I was cooking, the phone rang.

items.a: While cooking, I burnt my hand.
items.b: While cooking, the phone rang.
items.note: La segunda está mal: dice que el teléfono estaba cocinando.

items.a: Before going to bed, I read.
items.b: Before to go to bed, I read.
items.note: Después de before / after va -ing, nunca to + verbo.

items.a: After finishing, she left.
items.b: After having finished, she left.
items.note: Las dos son correctas; la forma perfecta remarca la secuencia.

branches.example: I left early because I felt sick.

branches.if: Una razón que el otro ya conoce
branches.example: Since you’re here, let’s start.

branches.use: if / as long as / provided that
branches.example: As long as it’s quiet, I can focus.
Unless I sleep well, I’m tired all day.
Take an umbrella in case it rains.

steps.label: Con if
steps.sentence: **If I don’t sleep** eight hours, I’m groggy.

steps.label: Con unless
steps.sentence: **Unless I sleep** eight hours, I’m groggy.
steps.change: “Unless” ya es negativo: no agregues otro “not”.

steps.label: Condición firme
steps.sentence: **As long as I sleep** eight hours, I’m fine.

items.a: Unless it rains, we’ll go.
items.b: Unless it doesn’t rain, we’ll go.
items.note: La segunda tiene doble negación: está mal.

items.a: As long as it stays quiet, I’ll finish.
items.b: As long as it will stay quiet, I’ll finish.
items.note: En la condición sobre el futuro, usa presente.

items.a: I’ll take a jacket if it’s cold.
items.b: I’ll take a jacket in case it’s cold.
items.note: La primera: solo si hace frío. La segunda: la llevo por si acaso.

branches.if: El carácter de la persona (kind, rude, generous, brave)
branches.example: It was kind of you to call.

branches.if: La dificultad o importancia (hard, easy, important)
branches.example: It’s hard for him to say sorry.

branches.if: Una acción en general, sin persona
branches.example: It’s rude to interrupt.
It’s a mistake to assume.

steps.label: General
steps.sentence: **It’s rude to** interrupt.
steps.change: It + adjetivo + to: juzga la acción.

steps.label: Con of
steps.sentence: **It was rude of him to** interrupt.

steps.label: Con for
steps.sentence: **It’s hard for him to** stop interrupting.
steps.change: “For” habla de la dificultad para esa persona.

steps.label: Con gerundio
steps.sentence: **Interrupting** is rude.
steps.change: Misma idea, más general y escrita.

B2-5-0.title: Of y for no son iguales

items.a: It was nice of you to help.
items.b: It was nice for you to help.
items.note: Con “nice” que juzga a la persona, se usa “of”.

items.a: It’s difficult for me to say no.
items.b: It’s difficult of me to say no.
items.note: La dificultad se expresa con “for”.

items.a: It’s important to listen.
items.b: Is important to listen.
items.note: En inglés el sujeto “It” es obligatorio.

B2-5-1.title: Del infinitivo español al gerundio inglés

steps.label: Español
steps.sentence: **Interrumpir** a la gente es de mala educación.

steps.label: Inglés natural
steps.sentence: **Interrupting** people **is** rude.
steps.change: El sujeto va en -ing y el verbo en singular.

steps.label: Negativo
steps.sentence: **Not answering** messages **is** rude.

steps.label: Alternativa con it
steps.sentence: **It’s** rude **to interrupt** people.
steps.change: Otra forma muy común en el habla.

branches.example: Listening saves time.

branches.if: Un comentario sobre la acción (más hablado)
branches.example: It’s useful to listen.
Listening and asking questions help.
What helps is listening.

items.a: Reading the reports takes time.
items.b: Reading the reports take time.
items.note: El sujeto es “reading” (singular), no “reports”.

items.a: Listening and asking help.
items.b: Listening and asking helps.
items.note: Dos gerundios unidos con “and” llevan verbo en plural.

items.a: Listening is a skill.
items.b: To listen is a skill.
items.note: El infinitivo como sujeto suena literario o anticuado.

B2-6-0.title: ¿Present perfect o pasado simple?
B2-6-0.question: ¿Cómo es el tiempo de la acción?

branches.if: Un momento terminado y conocido (yesterday, last night, in 2019, ago)
branches.example: The story broke last night.

branches.if: Tiempo no terminado (today, this week, so far)
branches.example: We’ve had three calls today.
Have you ever met a minister?

branches.if: Un resultado que se ve ahora
branches.example: She’s lost her notes, so she can’t check.

steps.label: Noticia (resultado actual)
steps.sentence: Reporters **have uncovered** new evidence.
steps.change: Present perfect: la noticia importa ahora.

steps.label: Detalle con fecha
steps.sentence: They **found** the documents **on Tuesday**.

steps.label: Desde entonces
steps.sentence: **Since then**, nobody **has commented**.

items.a: Have you ever been to Cartagena?
items.b: Did you go to Cartagena?
items.note: La primera pregunta por experiencia; la segunda, por una ocasión concreta.

items.a: I saw him yesterday.
items.b: I’ve seen him yesterday.
items.note: Con “yesterday” solo se usa el pasado simple.

items.a: She’s lost her keys.
items.b: She lost her keys.
items.note: La primera: todavía no las tiene. La segunda: solo cuenta lo que pasó.

branches.if: En el resultado o la cantidad (how many)
branches.example: I’ve read three reports.

branches.if: En la actividad y su duración (how long)
branches.example: I’ve been reading all day.
You’re red. Have you been running?

branches.if: Es un verbo de estado (know, own, believe)
branches.example: I’ve known her for years.

steps.label: Cantidad
steps.sentence: She **has written** three articles.
steps.change: Simple: el resultado se puede contar.

steps.label: Duración
steps.sentence: She **has been writing** since dawn.
steps.change: Continuo: la actividad y su duración.

steps.label: Juntos
steps.sentence: She**’s been writing** all day and **has finished** three articles.

items.a: I’ve painted the kitchen.
items.b: I’ve been painting the kitchen.
items.note: La primera: está terminado. La segunda: tal vez no he terminado y hay pintura por todos lados.

items.a: I’ve known him for years.
items.b: I’ve been knowing him for years.
items.note: “Know” es verbo de estado: no se usa en continuo.

items.a: I’ve lived here for six years.
items.b: I’ve been living here for six years.
items.note: Con live, work o study las dos son casi iguales.

steps.label: Already
steps.sentence: The crowd **had already left**.

steps.label: Just
steps.sentence: The editor **had just finished** when the news broke.

steps.label: Never
steps.sentence: He **had never spoken** to the press before.

steps.label: Yet
steps.sentence: The results **hadn’t arrived yet**.
steps.change: Al final, en negativas y preguntas.

items.a: When we arrived, they left.
items.b: When we arrived, they had left.
items.note: La primera: se fueron cuando llegamos. La segunda: ya se habían ido.

items.a: After she called, we published.
items.b: After she had called, we published.
items.note: Con “after” el orden es claro: el pasado perfecto es opcional.

items.a: He said, “I saw it.”
items.b: He said he had seen it.
items.note: En estilo indirecto, el pasado simple suele pasar a pasado perfecto.

branches.if: Algo terminó antes de otro momento del pasado
branches.use: by the time + pasado simple, had + participio
branches.example: By the time we arrived, the crowd had left.
I had just sat down when the phone rang.

branches.if: Algo nunca había pasado antes de ese momento
branches.example: She had never seen the sea before.
The results hadn’t come in yet.

steps.label: Con auxiliar
steps.sentence: You**’ve** seen the update, **haven’t you**?

steps.label: Sin auxiliar
steps.sentence: Technology **moves** fast, **doesn’t it**?

steps.label: Sujeto negativo
steps.sentence: **Nobody** reads the terms, **do they**?

steps.label: Con there
steps.sentence: **There aren’t** any settings, **are there**?

branches.if: Esperas que el otro esté de acuerdo
branches.example: It’s cold today, isn’t it? ↘

branches.if: No estás seguro y quieres confirmar
branches.example: You’ve paid the bill, haven’t you? ↗

B2-7-1.title: De opinión directa a pregunta negativa

steps.label: Opinión directa
steps.sentence: Children get phones too early.

steps.label: Invitar a estar de acuerdo
steps.sentence: **Don’t you think** children get phones too early?

steps.label: Sorpresa
steps.sentence: **Isn’t it** strange **how** early children get phones?
steps.change: Dentro de la cláusula, orden de afirmación.

steps.label: Propuesta suave
steps.sentence: **Wouldn’t it be** better to wait?

branches.example: Isn’t it amazing how fast it changed?
Don’t you think it’s too much?
Haven’t we all done that?
Wouldn’t it be simpler to ask?
Didn’t you check it?

B2-7-1.title: Cuidado con las respuestas y el tono

items.a: — Don’t you agree? — Yes.
items.b: — Don’t you agree? — No.
items.note: “Yes” significa que sí estás de acuerdo; “No”, que no lo estás.

items.a: Don’t you think so?
items.b: Do you not think so?
items.note: La forma sin contracción suena formal o molesta.

items.a: Isn’t it worrying how much they collect?
items.b: Isn’t it worrying how much do they collect?
items.note: Dentro de la cláusula no hay inversión.

B2-7-2.title: De activa a pasiva en tres tiempos

steps.label: Presente continuo
steps.sentence: They **are testing** the software. → The software **is being tested**.

steps.label: Present perfect
steps.sentence: They **have closed** the accounts. → The accounts **have been closed**.

steps.label: Futuro
steps.sentence: They **will publish** the report. → The report **will be published**.

steps.label: Agente con énfasis
steps.sentence: **A criminal group** has created the virus, not an amateur.
steps.change: Si el agente es la noticia, usa la activa.

B2-7-2.title: ¿Activa o pasiva?
B2-7-2.question: ¿Qué importancia tiene quién hace la acción?

branches.if: No se sabe quién lo hizo
branches.example: My account has been hacked.
The suspect is being questioned.
The report was leaked by the CEO himself.

branches.if: El agente es lo más importante
branches.example: A teenager created the virus.

items.a: More videos have been posted this year.
items.b: More videos have been being posted this year.
items.note: La pasiva del present perfect continuo casi no se usa: usa has / have been + participio.

items.a: The data is being collected.
items.b: The data is collecting.
items.note: Sin “being” + participio, parece que los datos recolectan algo.

items.a: It will be collected.
items.b: It will being collected.
items.note: En el futuro pasivo solo cambia “be”: will be + participio.

steps.label: Activa completa
steps.sentence: The people **who were waiting** outside were volunteers.

steps.label: Reducida con -ing
steps.sentence: The people **waiting** outside were volunteers.

steps.label: Pasiva completa
steps.sentence: The technique **that was used** by the team is simple.

steps.label: Reducida con participio
steps.sentence: The technique **used** by the team is simple.

steps.label: Verbo activo
steps.sentence: Anyone **who wants** to join → anyone **wanting** to join

B2-8-0.title: ¿Se puede reducir?
B2-8-0.question: ¿Qué función tiene el pronombre en la cláusula?

branches.if: Es sujeto y va con be + -ing
branches.example: the woman (who is) standing there

branches.if: Es sujeto y va con be + participio
branches.example: the study (that was) published in March

branches.if: Es sujeto con un verbo activo de estado o deseo
branches.example: anyone wanting to join

branches.use: no se reduce a -ing; solo puedes omitir el pronombre
branches.example: the professor (who) I interviewed

items.a: the book that I read
items.b: the book reading
items.note: Si el pronombre es objeto, no se puede reducir a -ing.

items.a: the study published in March
items.b: the study publishing in March
items.note: Sentido pasivo: participio, no -ing.

items.a: The man who broke the window ran away.
items.b: The man breaking the window ran away.
items.note: Con una acción puntual en pasado, la reducción a -ing suena rara.

steps.label: Dos frases
steps.sentence: He forgot my name. That was embarrassing.

steps.label: Con which
steps.sentence: He forgot my name, **which was embarrassing**.
steps.change: “Which” se refiere a toda la idea anterior.

steps.label: Consecuencia
steps.sentence: The bus was late, **which is why** I missed the meeting.
steps.change: “which is why” = razón por la cual.

steps.label: Resultado
steps.sentence: The data was lost, **which meant** starting again.

items.a: She left early, which surprised us.
items.b: She left early, what surprised us.
items.note: “Lo cual / lo que” para comentar una frase es “which”, nunca “what”.

items.a: She left early, which surprised us.
items.b: She left early which surprised us.
items.note: Sin coma, “which” parece referirse solo a la última palabra.

items.a: What surprised us was the delay.
items.b: Which surprised us was the delay.
items.note: Al inicio, como cláusula nominal, se usa “what”.

branches.example: He apologised, which was kind.
It rained, which is why we stayed in.
The flight was cancelled, which meant waiting a day.
Unlike my brother, I love mornings.
While some cultures value punctuality, others are relaxed.
The trip was perfect, except for the flight.

branches.if: Una excepción que es una oración
branches.example: It’s a great city, except that it rains a lot.

steps.label: Unlike
steps.sentence: **Unlike my parents**, I eat late.

steps.label: While
steps.sentence: **While my parents eat at six**, I eat at nine.

steps.label: Whereas (formal)
steps.sentence: My parents eat at six, **whereas I eat at nine**.

items.a: Unlike my brother, I get up early.
items.b: Unlike my brother gets up late, I get up early.
items.note: “Unlike” va con sustantivo, nunca con una oración.

items.a: While I was cooking, he called.
items.b: While I cook, he orders in.
items.note: “While” puede significar “mientras (al mismo tiempo)” o contraste; “whereas” solo contraste.

items.a: Everyone came except Marta.
items.b: Everyone came except that Marta.
items.note: “Except” + sustantivo; “except that” + oración.

branches.if: Un estado (be, have, live, like, know)
branches.example: I used to be shy.

branches.if: Una acción repetida en el pasado
branches.example: Every summer we used to / would go to the coast.

branches.if: Una sola acción en el pasado
branches.example: I went to Cartagena in 2010.

branches.if: Algo a lo que estás acostumbrado ahora
branches.example: I’m used to getting up early.

steps.label: Español
steps.sentence: Antes **vivíamos** junto al mar.

steps.label: Estado
steps.sentence: We **used to live** by the sea.

steps.label: Español
steps.sentence: Todos los veranos mi abuela nos **contaba** historias.

steps.label: Acción repetida
steps.sentence: Every summer my grandmother **would tell** us stories.
steps.change: Con acción repetida y marco de tiempo, “would” suena nostálgico.

items.a: I used to get up early.
items.b: I’m used to getting up early.
items.note: La primera: antes madrugaba. La segunda: estoy acostumbrado a madrugar.

items.a: I used to have a dog.
items.b: I would have a dog.
items.note: “Have” (posesión) es estado: solo “used to”.

items.a: Did you use to play?
items.b: Did you used to play?
items.note: En preguntas y negativas se escribe “use to”, sin -d.

items.a: What annoys me is the noise.
items.b: The noise that annoys me is next door.
items.note: La primera es una cláusula nominal (sujeto); la segunda describe “the noise”.

items.a: I know what you bought.
items.b: I know the shop that you bought it in.
items.note: “What” = lo que; “that” describe un sustantivo que ya aparece.

items.a: What I need is a refund.
items.b: That what I need is a refund.
items.note: “What” ya significa “lo que”: no agregues “that”.

steps.label: Queja simple
steps.sentence: The delivery never arrived.

steps.label: Con what
steps.sentence: **What annoys me is that** the delivery never arrived.
steps.change: La cláusula con “what” es el sujeto.

steps.label: Con the thing that
steps.sentence: **The thing that bothers me is that** the delivery never arrived.

steps.label: Con petición
steps.sentence: **What I’d like is** a full refund.
steps.change: Sirve para pedir algo con firmeza.

branches.if: Funciona como sujeto u objeto (= lo que)
branches.example: What surprised me was the price.

branches.if: Funciona como objeto con una pregunta indirecta
branches.use: cláusula nominal con why / how / where
branches.example: I don’t understand why they charged me twice.

branches.if: Describe un sustantivo que ya está en la frase
branches.use: cláusula relativa con that / which / who
branches.example: The product that I bought is faulty.

steps.label: Directa
steps.sentence: Where **is** the manager?

steps.label: Indirecta
steps.sentence: Could you tell me where **the manager is**?

steps.label: Directa con did
steps.sentence: Why **did** they charge me twice?

steps.label: Indirecta
steps.sentence: I’d like to know why **they charged** me twice.
steps.change: Desaparece “did” y el verbo va en pasado.

steps.label: Sí / no
steps.sentence: **Is** there a refund policy? → Do you know **if there is** a refund policy?

items.example: Do you know when it opens?
Could you tell me where it is?
Do you happen to know if it’s open?
Would you mind telling me why?
I was wondering whether you could help.

items.a: Could you tell me where it is?
items.b: I was wondering where it is.
items.note: Si empieza con “Could you…”, lleva signo de pregunta; con “I was wondering…”, punto.

items.a: Do you know what it costs?
items.b: Do you know what does it cost?
items.note: Elimina do / does / did en la pregunta indirecta.

items.a: I don’t know whether or not it’s free.
items.b: I don’t know if or not it’s free.
items.note: Antes de “or not” solo se usa “whether”.

B2-11-0.title: ¿If, unless, only if o even if?
B2-11-0.question: ¿Qué relación tiene la condición con el resultado?

branches.example: If I had more time, I’d volunteer.

branches.if: El resultado ocurre si la condición NO se cumple
branches.example: I wouldn’t lie unless I had to.
I’d agree only if it were public.
Even if they paid me, I’d refuse.
If I were you, I’d tell the truth.

items.example: If I asked, she might agree.
If I had a car, I could drive you.
If I had time, I’d help.

items.a: If I have time, I’ll help.
items.b: If I had time, I’d help.
items.note: La primera es una posibilidad real; la segunda, una situación imaginaria.

items.a: If I were you, I’d apologise.
items.b: If I would be you, I’d apologise.
items.note: En la cláusula con “if” no se usa “would”.

items.a: Unless you ask, nobody will help.
items.b: Unless you don’t ask, nobody will help.
items.note: “Unless” ya es negativo: no agregues “don’t”.

branches.if: Sobre el presente (algo que no es así ahora)
branches.example: I wish I had more free time.

branches.if: Sobre un estado o tu identidad
branches.example: I wish I were braver.
I wish I had said sorry.

branches.if: Sobre lo que otra persona hace y te molesta
branches.example: I wish people wouldn’t drop litter.
I wish I could drive.

steps.label: Realidad presente
steps.sentence: I **don’t have** a car.

steps.label: Deseo presente
steps.sentence: I wish I **had** a car.

steps.label: Realidad pasada
steps.sentence: I **didn’t say** sorry.

steps.label: Arrepentimiento
steps.sentence: If only I **had said** sorry.

items.a: I wish I could stop smoking.
items.b: I wish I would stop smoking.
items.note: Sobre ti mismo no se usa “would”; usa “could”.

items.a: I wish I had more time.
items.b: I wish I have more time.
items.note: Después de “wish” para el presente, usa pasado.

items.a: I wish you would call more.
items.b: I hope you call more.
items.note: “Wish + would” es una queja; “hope” es una esperanza real.

B2-12-0.title: ¿Futuro perfecto simple o continuo?
B2-12-0.question: ¿Qué quieres resaltar en ese punto del futuro?

branches.if: Que la acción ya estará terminada
branches.example: By six I’ll have finished.
By then I’ll have visited five countries.
By June I’ll have been travelling for six months.

branches.if: Un verbo de estado (know, be, have)
branches.example: By May I’ll have known her for ten years.

B2-12-0.title: Mira hacia atrás desde el futuro

steps.label: Plan
steps.sentence: I’m going to finish the course.

steps.label: Terminado para una fecha
steps.sentence: **By December I’ll have finished** the course.

steps.label: Duración hasta esa fecha
steps.sentence: By December **I’ll have been studying** for two years.

steps.label: Con by the time
steps.sentence: **By the time you arrive**, we’ll have eaten.

items.a: By the time you arrive, we’ll have left.
items.b: By the time you will arrive, we’ll have left.
items.note: Después de “by the time” va presente.

items.a: I’ll have known her for ten years.
items.b: I’ll have been knowing her for ten years.
items.note: “Know” no se usa en continuo.

items.a: By 2030 I’ll have retired.
items.b: In 2030 I’ll have retired.
items.note: “By” marca la fecha límite; con el futuro perfecto es lo más natural.

B2-12-1.title: ¿Qué tipo de condicional mixto?
B2-12-1.question: ¿De qué tiempo es la causa y de qué tiempo es el resultado?

branches.if: Causa en el pasado → resultado en el presente
branches.example: If I had saved more, I’d be travelling now.

branches.if: Causa permanente en el presente → resultado en el pasado
branches.use: If + pasado simple, would have + participio
branches.example: If I weren’t so shy, I would have spoken up.

branches.if: Las dos en el pasado (tercer condicional)
branches.use: If + past perfect, would have + participio
branches.example: If I’d known, I’d have called.

branches.if: Las dos en el presente (segundo condicional)
branches.example: If I had time, I’d go.

steps.label: Hecho pasado
steps.sentence: I **didn’t take** the job in Bogotá.

steps.label: Consecuencia presente
steps.sentence: If I **had taken** the job, I **would be living** in Bogotá **now**.

steps.label: Rasgo permanente
steps.sentence: I**’m** not very organised.

steps.label: Consecuencia pasada
steps.sentence: If I **were** more organised, I **wouldn’t have missed** the flight.

items.a: If I’d studied, I’d have passed.
items.b: If I’d studied, I’d be a doctor now.
items.note: La primera tiene resultado en el pasado; la segunda, en el presente.

items.a: If she were braver, she’d have asked.
items.b: If she had been braver, she’d have asked.
items.note: La primera habla de su carácter permanente; la segunda, de ese momento.

items.a: If we’d left earlier, we’d be there by now.
items.b: If we’d left earlier, we’ll be there by now.
items.note: En el resultado hipotético va “would”, no “will”.
